\begin{equation} \label{desi.2}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |x|^\beta |u|^{p-2}uv\,dx  \leq \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |x|^\frac{\beta(p-1)}{p} |u|^{p-1} |x|^\frac{\beta}{p}v\,dx  \leq \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |x|^\beta |u|^p\,dx\right)^\frac{p-1}{p}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |x|^\beta |v|^p\right)^\frac{1}{p}.
\end{equation}
Hence, from \eqref{desi.0}, \eqref{desi.1} and \eqref{desi.2}, we get that the operator $\mathcal{\tilde L}$ defined as
$$
\langle  \mathcal{\tilde L}_{s,p,\gamma} u,v\rangle := \langle \mathcal{L}_{s,p,\gamma}\, u,v\rangle + \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |x|^\beta |u|^{p-2}uv\,dx 
$$
fulfills the following relation
$$
\langle  \mathcal{\tilde L}_{s,p,\gamma} u,v \rangle \leq C\|u\|_{s,p,\beta}^{p-1} \|v\|_{s,p,\beta}.
$$
Moreover, by definition
$$
\langle  \mathcal{\tilde L}_{s,p,\gamma} u,v \rangle = \langle \mathcal{L}_{s,p,\gamma}\, u,u\rangle + \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |x|^\beta |u|^{p}\,dx \leq C\|u\|_{s,p,\beta}^p.
$$
Therefore, in light of Proposition \ref{S.prop}, the operator  $\mathcal{\tilde L}_{s,p,\gamma}$ satisfies the (S)-property of compactness according to Definition \ref{def.S.prop}.

\end{remark}

\section{Boundedness of solutions}\label{B}
In this section, we prove that any radial solution 
u of problem \eqref{eq}  is bounded. 

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{teo_boundedness}] In what follows, we will apply a De Giorgi's iteration scheme to control the level sets of a solution $u$ to problem \eqref{eq}.

For a positive integer $k$, define
$$w_{k}:= (u-(1-2^{-k}))_{+}.$$Then, as in \cite{FP}, the following holds
\begin{equation}\label{property w}
w_{k+1} \leq w_k \text{ in }\mathbb{R}^N, \quad u(x)< (2^{k+1}-1)w_k \text{ in }\left\lbrace w_{k+1}>0\right\rbrace, \quad \text{and }\left\lbrace w_{k+1}>0\right\rbrace \subset \left\lbrace w_{k}>2^{-(k+1)}\right\rbrace. 
\end{equation}

post_theorem_intro_text:
The proof of Theorem \ref{teo.1} relies mainly on establishing a suitable compact embedding of the fractional Sobolev space of weighted radial functions into an appropriate weighted Lebesgue space (see Theorem \ref{compact}). This compactness result is the key ingredient that enables the application of a Mountain Pass–type existence theorem (see Lemma \ref{lema.BN}).

We note that our result extends the existence obtained in \cite{PdN, Sin,Ma} to the setting of local-nonlocal nonlinear operators on unbounded domains. Furthermore, the range of parameters given in \eqref{cond exponent 2} improves upon that obtained in \cite{Ma} in the particular case  $p=2$ and $\beta=2$.

\medskip
Regarding regularity, in the following result, by employing a De Giorgi's iteration scheme, we find that radial weak solutions of \eqref{eq} are indeed bounded.

\begin{theorem} \label{teo_boundedness}
Let $s\in (0,1]$ be such that $1/p<s<N/p$,  $\alpha>-sp $ and $p<q<p^{*}_{\gamma, s, \alpha}$. Moreover, assume condition \eqref{cond exponent 2}. Then, for any radial weak   solution $u$ to \eqref{eq}, there is a constant $C>0$ such that
$$\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^N)}\leq C.$$
\end{theorem}

Finally, by applying a generalization of Pohozaev’s existence result established in \cite{ROS}, we show that the value $\frac{p(N+\alpha)}{N-sp}$ serves as a threshold for the existence of bounded solutions with a weighted control of the gradient.

\begin{theorem} \label{teo.no.exist}
Let $s\in (0,1]$ be such that $1/p<s<N/p$, $\alpha>-sp$ and  $\beta>p(1-s)$. Then, for all $q>p^{*}_{\gamma, s, \alpha}$, problem \eqref{eq} has no solutions $u\in \mathcal{\tilde X}(\mathbb{R}^N)$, being
$$
\mathcal{\tilde X}(\mathbb{R}^N) =\{ u \in \mathcal{W}^{s,p}_\beta(\mathbb{R}^N)\cap L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^N) \text{ such that } |\nabla u(x)||x| \in L^r(\mathbb{R}^N) \text{ for some } r>1\}.
$$
\end{theorem} 

\bigskip

The paper is organized as follows. In Section \ref{sec.1} we provide the functional framework and preliminary definitions. In the next Section \ref{sec.2}, we quote the main properties of radial functions related to our problem,    specially, Strauss' type lemmas, generalized Rother's Lemma and  compactness of embeddings between fractional Sobolev spaces of radial functions and appropriate Lebesgue weighted spaces. In Section \ref{sec.3}, we state the existence of solutions to problem \eqref{eq} through variational methods, and in Section \ref{B} we prove the boundedness of radial solutions. Finally, Section \ref{sec.6} is devoted to prove our non-existence result. For convenience of the reader, we add an Appendix with the Brezis-Nirenberg version of the Mountain Pass Theorem and some monotonicity properties of operators that we employ in the paper.

theorem.label: thm:main

post_theorem_intro_text:
This improves the aforementioned asymptotic results of Mycroft and Z\'arate-Guer\'en~\cite{mycroft2025positive}, who showed that $\delta^*(G) \ge (1 - 1/t)n + o(n)$ suffices. Our methods are largely different from theirs. Our analysis splits into two regimes: the extremal and non-extremal (see \Cref{sec:stability} for details). The extremal regime does not feature in \cite{mycroft2025positive} at all, and for this we use ad-hoc structural analysis with lemmas about random matchings in bipartite graphs and about finding almost spanning subhypergraphs with large minimum supported codegree in almost complete hypergraphs. For the non-extremal case, while Mycroft and Z\'arate-Guer\'en rely on a version of the regularity lemma for hypergraphs (called the weak regularity lemma) along with the absorption method, our approach stems from Lang's breakthrough work \cite{lang2023tiling} on hypergraph tilings, which allows us to completely avoid the regularity lemma and greatly simplifies the use of the absorption method. For the latter part, however, we use a novel idea from \cite{mycroft2025positive} about weighted fractional matchings that, coupled with Farkas' linear-algebraic lemma, allows one to find spanning $\ell$-cycles in certain $k$-partite $k$-graphs, which is one of the steps in our proof. 

We point out that Illingworth, Lang, M\"uyesser, Parczyk and Sgueglia~\cite{illingworth2025spanning} conjectured that for all $k\ge 3$, any sufficiently large $k$-graph with $\delta^*(G) \ge (1-1/k)n$ contains a tight Hamilton cycle, which is a special case of \cref{thm:main} (up to the $k-3$ term). Observe that if $k$ divides $n$, then a tight Hamilton cycle in $G$ will contain a perfect matching. Thus, our result implies that $\delta^*(G) \ge (1 - 1/k)n - (k-3)$ ensures a perfect matching, which recovers a result of Mycroft and Z\'arate-Guer\'en~\cite{mycroft2025matching} up to an additive constant of one, who show that a bound of $(1 - 1/k)n - (k - 2)$ suffices.

As alluded to above, the bound in \cref{thm:main} is off by one in most cases. In fact, in many cases (namely whenever $t \ge \ell+2$ or when $\ell = k-1$, that is, we are seeking a tight Hamilton cycle), our techniques can be adapted to prove \cref{thm:main} with the improved bound of $\delta^*(G) \ge (1 - 1/t)n - (k - 2)$ instead (which, for instance, would immediately imply the previously discussed optimal perfect matching bound). 
However, since this will require some technical modifications, we choose to present a single unified proof for $\delta^*(G) \ge (1 - 1/t)n - (k - 3)$ that will work for all cases instead. We point out the part of our proof that requires the exact degree condition in \Cref{rem:exact degree}, and briefly discuss how to suitably alter our proof and remove the extra one in the bound in all relevant cases in \Cref{sec:improving the bound}.

Finally, we remark that in a recent personal communication, Mycroft and Z\'arate-Guer\'en informed us that they are preparing a manuscript where they prove that any sufficiently large $3$-graph with no isolated vertices and $\delta^*(G) \ge n/2$ contains a loose Hamilton cycle. This improves the previous asymptotic bound of $n/2 + o(n)$ established by them~\cite{mycroft2025positive} and Halfpap and Magnan~\cite{halfpap2024positive} (which our methods can recover as well) and extends \cref{thm:main} to include $(k,\ell) = (3,1)$, the only case we do not handle.

\paragraph{Organisation of the paper.} In \Cref{sec:overview}, we first provide lower bound constructions to prove the optimality of \cref{thm:main}. We then split the proof of \cref{thm:main} into two complementary cases and handle them separately in \cref{thm:Hamilton cycle non-extremal,thm:Hamilton cycle extremal}. We also provide brief proof overviews for both these theorems in \Cref{sec:proof-overviews}. Then in \Cref{sec:prelims} we introduce some notation and definitions and provide some basic tools.

\Crefrange{sec:non-extremal}{sec:proof Hamilton paths} are dedicated to proving \cref{thm:Hamilton cycle non-extremal}, and \Crefrange{sec:extremal hypergraphs}{sec:Hamilton cycle extremal} prove \cref{thm:Hamilton cycle extremal}. These two parts are treated largely independently, and can be read as such. We conclude with some open problems in \Cref{sec:conclusion}.

mcq.question:
Fix integers $k$ and $\ell$ with $k\ge 3$, $1\le \ell\le k-1$, and $(k,\ell)\ne (3,1)$. Let
\[
 t = \Big\lfloor \frac{k}{k-\ell}\Big\rfloor (k-\ell),
\]
and let $n$ be sufficiently large and divisible by $k-\ell$. Suppose $H$ is a $k$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices with no isolated vertices and with minimum supported co-degree at least $(1-1/t)n-(k-3)$. Which statement correctly asserts what must exist under these assumptions?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: The hypergraph $H$ contains a Hamilton $\ell$-cycle (i.e., there exists a Hamilton $\ell$-cycle in $H$).

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hypergraph $H$ contains a Hamilton $(k-\ell)$-cycle (that is, a spanning cycle in which consecutive edges intersect in exactly $k-\ell$ vertices).

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hypergraph $H$ contains an $\ell$-cycle that spans all but at most $k-\ell$ vertices of $H$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hypergraph $H$ contains a Hamilton $\ell$-cycle provided only that $n$ is sufficiently large (without assuming that $n$ is divisible by $k-\ell$).

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hypergraph $H$ contains a Hamilton $\ell$-cycle already under the weaker bound that the minimum supported co-degree is at least $(1-1/t)n-(k-2)$.

\label{theo:weightLp}  Let $2< p<+\infty$ and $\gamma\in (0,2)$.  Let $\vu_0\in L^p(\mathbb{R}^3, \frac{dx}{1+\vert x\vert^2})$ with $\mathrm{div}\, \vu_0=0$. Then the Navier\ddh Stokes equations
  \begin{equation}\label{NSEq3} \left\{ \begin{split} \partial_t\vu=&\Delta\vu -\mathbb{P}\Div(\vu\otimes\vu))
\\\Div\,\vu=&0  \\ \lim_{t\rightarrow 0} \vu(t,.)=&\vu_0\end{split}\right.\end{equation} have a solution on $(0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3$ with, for every $0<T<+\infty$, 
$\vu\in L^\infty((0,T), L^2(\frac{dx}{1+\vert x\vert^2}))+ L^\infty((0,T), L^r)$ for some $r\in (3,+\infty)$.
theorem.label: theo:weightLp

post_theorem_intro_text: The limit case $L^\infty((0,T), L^2(\frac{dx}{1+\vert x\vert^2}))$ corresponds to the results of Fern\'andez-Dalgo \&  Lemari\'e-Rieusset \cite{FLR20} and Bradshaw, Kucavica \& Tsai \cite{BKT22}. The limit case $L^\infty((0,T),L^r)$ corresponds to Kato's mild solutions in $L^r$  \cite{Kat84}  (existence of mild solutions  is known only for a finite time $T\approx \frac 1{\|\vu_0\|_r^{\frac{2r}{r-3}}}$).  In order to deal with the case $2<p<+\infty$, we shall use Calder\'on's method  \cite{Cal90} and  split the initial value in a sum of two vector fields corresponding to the limit cases which we know how to deal with.

mcq.question: Let \(2<p<+\infty\) and \(\gamma\in(0,2)\). Let \(\mathbf{u}_0\in L^p(\mathbb{R}^3,\frac{dx}{1+|x|^2})\) with \(\mathrm{div}\,\mathbf{u}_0=0\). Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes system on \((0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3\): \(\partial_t\mathbf{u}=\Delta\mathbf{u}-\mathbb{P}\,\mathrm{Div}(\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{u})\), \(\mathrm{Div}\,\mathbf{u}=0\), and \(\lim_{t\to0}\mathbf{u}(t,\cdot)=\mathbf{u}_0\). Under these assumptions, which statement correctly asserts the existence of a solution with the stated spacetime bounds?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: There exists a solution \(\mathbf{u}\) on \((0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3\) satisfying \(\partial_t\mathbf{u}=\Delta\mathbf{u}-\mathbb{P}\,\mathrm{Div}(\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{u})\), \(\mathrm{Div}\,\mathbf{u}=0\), and \(\lim_{t\to0}\mathbf{u}(t,\cdot)=\mathbf{u}_0\), and such that for every \(0<T<+\infty\), \(\mathbf{u}\in L^\infty((0,T);L^2(\mathbb{R}^3,\frac{dx}{1+|x|^2}))+L^\infty((0,T);L^r(\mathbb{R}^3))\) for some \(r\in(3,+\infty)\).

choices.label: B
choices.text: There exists a solution \(\mathbf{u}\) on \((0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3\) satisfying \(\partial_t\mathbf{u}=\Delta\mathbf{u}-\mathbb{P}\,\mathrm{Div}(\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{u})\), \(\mathrm{Div}\,\mathbf{u}=0\), and \(\lim_{t\to0}\mathbf{u}(t,\cdot)=\mathbf{u}_0\), and such that for every \(0<T<+\infty\), one has the uniform bound \(\mathbf{u}\in L^\infty((0,T);L^2(\mathbb{R}^3,\tfrac{dx}{1+|x|^2}))\cap L^\infty((0,T);L^r(\mathbb{R}^3))\) for some \(r\in(3,+\infty)\).

choices.label: C
choices.text: There exists a solution \(\mathbf{u}\) on \((0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3\) satisfying \(\partial_t\mathbf{u}=\Delta\mathbf{u}-\mathbb{P}\,\mathrm{Div}(\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{u})\), \(\mathrm{Div}\,\mathbf{u}=0\), and \(\lim_{t\to0}\mathbf{u}(t,\cdot)=\mathbf{u}_0\), and such that for every \(0<T<+\infty\), \(\mathbf{u}\in L^\infty((0,T);L^2(\mathbb{R}^3,\tfrac{dx}{1+|x|^2}))+L^\infty((0,T);L^r(\mathbb{R}^3))\) for some \(r\in[3,+\infty)\).

choices.label: D
choices.text: For every divergence-free \(\mathbf{u}_0\in L^p(\mathbb{R}^3,\tfrac{dx}{1+|x|^2})\) with \(2<p<+\infty\), there exists a solution \(\mathbf{u}\) on \((0,+\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3\) satisfying \(\partial_t\mathbf{u}=\Delta\mathbf{u}-\mathbb{P}\,\mathrm{Div}(\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{u})\), \(\mathrm{Div}\,\mathbf{u}=0\), and \(\lim_{t\to0}\mathbf{u}(t,\cdot)=\mathbf{u}_0\), and such that for every \(0<T<+\infty\) and every \(r\in(3,+\infty)\) one has \(\mathbf{u}\in L^\infty((0,T);L^2(\mathbb{R}^3,\tfrac{dx}{1+|x|^2}))+L^\infty((0,T);L^r(\mathbb{R}^3))\).

post_theorem_intro_text:
\begin{remark}\label{remcf}
	It is clear that $f\in C^{\alpha}(\rn\setminus\mathcal{O})$. Moreover, the viscosity solution $u$ in Theorem \ref{thm1} 
	is really $C^{2,\alpha}$ near infinity, see Section 3.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}\label{rembeta}
	The assumption $\beta>2$ is essentially optimal, one can see the example in \cite{blz,tz}.
\end{remark}

The major difficulties in this paper are caused by the lower regularity and the aperiodicity of $f$. To get the asymptotic behavior near infinity, 
the authors both in \cite{cl2} and \cite{tz} paid much attention on the second-order increment of $u$. Their vital step is deducing a suitable 
equation of the increment. More specifically, in \cite{cl2}, although $f$ is just H\"{o}lder continuous they obtained a homogeneous equation of the increment 
since $f$ is periodic, while in \cite{tz} the authors got a nonhomogeneous equation in which the nonhomogeneous term can be controlled since the higher 
regularity of $f$. 
In the case $f\in L^\infty$ is periodic \cite{ll}, the authors established the asymptotic results by following the main ideas in 
\cite{cl2} with additional approximation arguments. 
It is not the case in our paper and the second-order increment is not an appropriate object for us. We will propose a novel 
fractional order increment and deduce a nonhomogeneous equation of it. Then we employ the nonlocal ideas in \cite{qb} and refine the 
nonlocal method to measure the decay of the nonhomogeneous term. The asymptotic behavior is finally established with the aid of the fractional order increment.

\subsection*{Notations and the structure of the article}

Throughout the paper, we use the following notations:

The point $x\in\rn$ will also be written as $x=(x_1,x')=(x_1,\cdots,x_n)$. The notation $|x|$ denotes the Euclidean norm of $x$.
$B_r(x)\subset\rn$ denotes the ball centered at $x$ with radius $r$. 
We drop the center if it coincides with the origin, i.e., $B_r=B_r(0)$. 

The identity matrix is denoted by $I$. 
For an $n\times n$ matrix $B=(b_{ij})_{n\times n}$, $1\leq i,j\leq n$, $cof_{ij}B$ stands for the algebraic cofactor of 
element $b_{ij}$. We will always assume that $i,j\in\mathbb{N}_+$ and $i,j\leq n$ in this paper 
except for additional explanation.

Given a function $u:\rn\rightarrow{\mathbb R}$ and a point $x\in\rn$, we denote by $Du(x)$ and $\Delta u(x)$ the gradient  vector and 
the  Laplacian respectively.  

Let $k\in\mathbb{N}$, $\kappa\in(0,1)$ and $\Omega\subset\rn$ be open. For multi-indices 
$\gamma=(\gamma_1,\cdots,\gamma_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n$, we let $|\gamma|$ denote the sum of its components. 
The space $C^k(\overline{\Omega})$ consists of functions $u: \overline{\Omega}\rightarrow{\mathbb R}$, which admit derivatives 
up to order $k$, such that \begin{equation*}
	\|u\|_{C^{k}(\overline{\Omega})}:=\sup_{\substack{ \gamma\in\mathbb{N}^n\\|\gamma|\leq k}}
	\sup_{x\in{\Omega}}\left|D^\gamma u(x)\right|<+\infty.\end{equation*}
The H\"{o}lder space $C^{k,\kappa}(\overline{\Omega})$ consists of function $u\in C^k(\overline{\Omega})$ satisfying 
\begin{gather*}
	\|u\|_{C^{k,\kappa}(\overline{\Omega})}:=\|u\|_{C^{k}(\overline{\Omega})}+[u]_{C^{k,\kappa}(\overline{\Omega})}<+\infty, 
\end{gather*} 
where the seminorm 
\begin{equation*}
	[u]_{C^{k,\kappa}(\overline{\Omega})}:=\sup_{\substack{ \gamma\in\mathbb{N}^n\\|\gamma|=k}}
	\sup_{\substack{x,y\in{\Omega} \\ x\neq y}}\frac{|D^\gamma u(x)-D^\gamma u(y)|}{|x-y|^\kappa}.
\end{equation*}
A function $u\in C^{k,\kappa}_{loc}({\Omega})$ if $u\in C^{k,\kappa}(K)$ for all compact 
$K\subset\Omega$. For convenience, we may write $C^{0}(\overline{\Omega})$, $C^{k,\kappa}(\overline{\Omega})$ as $C(\overline{\Omega})$, 
$C^{k+\kappa}(\overline{\Omega})$,  respectively. 

The paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we introduce the fractional Laplacian and a series of relevant properties,  
which will be applied in the sequel. In Section 3, we deduce the equation for the fractional order increment (Lemma \ref{lemeqv}) and then 
show the crucial estimate (Lemma \ref{lemeF}) by a nonlocal method. Finally, Theorem \ref{thm1} is proved in Section 4.

theorem.content:
\label{thm:main}
    For any sequence of binary alphabet $\A_1,\A_2,\dots$, there exists an infinite cube-free word in $\A_1\times\A_2\times\dots$.
theorem.label: thm:main

post_theorem_intro_text:
In fact, we do not prove this result directly, but we prove two different stronger results, each implying Theorem \ref{thm:main}. 
These two proofs share a key idea: we can use an automaton to study the variant of the problem where we only forbid cubes of length at most $p$, for some arbitrary choice of $p$. Intuitively, short cubes are more difficult to avoid than long cubes, so by taking $p$ large enough, we should obtain a good approximation of the problem. Adapting standard tools from combinatorics on words and automata theory, studying this approximation is quite simple to achieve.
The delicate part is then to prove that if $p$ is large enough this approximation is good enough to deduce something about the original problem where all cubes are forbidden. 

The idea behind the first proof is to show that the growth rate of the language is not far from the growth rate of the regular approximation of the language which yields the following result.
\begin{theorem} \label{thm:growth}  
For any sequence of binary alphabet $\A_1,\A_2,\dots$, and for every $n$, there exist at least $1.35^n$ cube-free words in $\A_1\times\A_2\times\dots\times\A_n$. 
\end{theorem}
The core idea allowing us to deduce bounds on the growth of a power-free language $\mathcal L$ from its approximation $\mathcal L$ was first used by Kolpakov to estimate the growth rate of power-free languages \cite{kopakov2007efficient,Kolpakov2007Dec}. Shur later improved upon this technique \cite{shur2010Jul,Shur2012Nov}. This technique was later adapted by the second author to provide a partial answer to Conjecture \ref{conj:ThueListe} in  \cite{rosenfeld2022avoiding}.
The proof of this result applies the technique developed in \cite{rosenfeld2022avoiding} for squares, but provides a complete answer in the case of cubes.
The second proof of our main result does not imply anything about the number of solutions, but it contains algorithmic implications.
\begin{theorem} \label{thm:computable}
Let $\A_1,\A_2,\dots$ be a computable sequence of binary alphabet. Then there exists a computable infinite cube-free word $w=w_1w_2w_3\ldots$ in $\A_1\times\A_2\times\dots$. Moreover, there is an algorithm that given $w_1\ldots w_n$ and\ $\A_{n+1}$ computes $w_{n+1}$ in time polynomial in $n$.
\end{theorem}
This proof also relies on computing properties of the same automaton, but then we use a different argument for adding the large cubes back.
Intuitively, the idea is to introduce a weight function that measures how difficult it is to extend a word, and to prove that under some condition if the weight is not too large then at least one of the extensions also has a small weight (which we can then use inductively to construct a word). This idea was originally due to Miller \cite{miller2012two}, and was recently generalized in \cite{Rosenfeld2025Mar}. However, the weight functions in \cite{miller2012two} and \cite{Rosenfeld2025Mar} are much simpler and in our article the precise definition of the function depends on the automaton. Our result is in fact even stronger, as everything still holds if for all $i$ an opponent is allowed to choose the alphabet $\A_{i+1}$ after we choose $w_i$.

Note that Theorem \ref{thm:growth} and Theorem \ref{thm:computable} both independently imply Theorem \ref{thm:main}, but none of them seem to imply the other. We discuss the possible connection between this result in Section \ref{sec:discussion}.

The article is organized as follows. In Section \ref{sec:notation}, we introduce some common notations. In particular, we define the language $\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}^{(p)}$ that approximate the language of cube-free words, and we give the statement of Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvector} that is later crucial to our two proofs. In Section \ref{sec:potential}, we prove Theorem \ref{thm:computable}. In Section \ref{sec:growth}, we prove Theorem \ref{thm:growth}. Finally, we provide in Section \ref{sec:computations} a short description of the computation used to verify Lemma \ref{lem:eigenvector}.
sketch:
We "do not prove this result directly", but instead prove "two different stronger results, each implying Theorem \ref{thm:main}".

Both proofs share the idea to "use an automaton" to study an approximation where one "only forbid cubes of length at most $p$". Since "short cubes are more difficult to avoid than long cubes", taking $p$ large should give "a good approximation"; then, using "standard tools from combinatorics on words and automata theory", studying this approximation is "quite simple". The "delicate part" is to show that for $p$ large enough, this approximation is "good enough" to say something about the original problem where *all* cubes are forbidden.

First route (via growth): show that "the growth rate of the language is not far from the growth rate of the regular approximation of the language", yielding Theorem~\ref{thm:growth}; this uses the technique (Kolpakov/Shur, adapted in \cite{rosenfeld2022avoiding}) to "deduce bounds on the growth of a power-free language" from its approximation.

Second route (via constructivity): again compute properties of the same automaton, but then use "a different argument for adding the large cubes back"; namely, "introduce a weight function that measures how difficult it is to extend a word", and prove that under a condition, if the weight is small then "at least one of the extensions also has a small weight", enabling an inductive construction (as in Miller, generalized in \cite{Rosenfeld2025Mar}), yielding Theorem~\ref{thm:computable}.

Finally, "Theorem \ref{thm:growth} and Theorem \ref{thm:computable} both independently imply Theorem \ref{thm:main}".

\label{thm:main}
For any sequence of binary alphabet $\A_1,\A_2,\dots$, there exists an infinite cube-free word in $\A_1\times\A_2\times\dots$.

mcq.question: Let \(\mathcal A_1,\mathcal A_2,\dots\) be an arbitrary sequence of binary alphabets (each alphabet has exactly two symbols). Under these assumptions, which statement asserts the existence of an object with the specified avoidance property?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: There exists an infinite cube-free word over the alphabet \(\mathcal A_1\times\mathcal A_2\times\cdots\) (i.e., an infinite word with no factor of the form \(uuu\) with \(u\neq\varepsilon\)).

choices.label: B
choices.text: There exists a constant $p_0$ such that for every sequence of binary alphabet $\A_1,\A_2,\dots$, any infinite word in $\A_1\times\A_2\times\cdots$ that avoids all cubes $uuu$ with $|u|\le p_0$ is automatically cube-free (i.e., avoids $uuu$ for all nonempty $u$).

choices.label: C
choices.text: For every sequence of binary alphabet $\A_1,\A_2,\dots$ and every $n\ge 1$, there exists a cube-free word of length $n$ in $\A_1\times\A_2\times\cdots\times\A_n$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: For every sequence of binary alphabet $\A_1,\A_2,\dots$, there exists a computable infinite cube-free word $w=w_1w_2\cdots$ in $\A_1\times\A_2\times\cdots$, and moreover there is an algorithm that given $w_1\cdots w_n$ and $\A_{n+1}$ computes $w_{n+1}$ in time polynomial in $n$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For every sequence of binary alphabet $\A_1,\A_2,\dots$, there exists $c>1$ such that for every $n$ there are at least $c^n$ cube-free words in $\A_1\times\A_2\times\cdots\times\A_n$.

sketch_usage_meta.label: C
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: drop-infinite-existence; keep finite-length existence

sketch_usage_meta.label: D
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: drop computability hypothesis on $(\A_i)$ while keeping computable output

sketch_usage_meta.label: E
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: uniform exponential base c for all sequences (vs fixed 1.35 from approximation analysis)

ALS.justification: The stem does not give away which option is correct, and it does not restate the correct choice’s content verbatim. The phrase “existence of an object with the specified avoidance property” is generic and applies to multiple options.

TAS.justification: The question is essentially asking the test-taker to recognize the right existence assertion among several related-looking existence/avoidance statements. This is close to a meta-restatement (“which statement asserts existence…”) rather than requiring engagement with the combinatorics of cube-freeness.

GPS.justification: Some reasoning about quantifiers/strength is needed (e.g., distinguishing plain existence from uniform cutoffs, effectivity, and exponential counting). However, the task is largely classification of statement strength/meaning rather than deriving a conclusion from mathematical constraints.

DQS.justification: Distractors are plausible and target common failure modes: (B) a tempting but generally false uniform finite-check cutoff, (C) a weaker finite-length existence, (D) an over-strong computability/polynomial-time extension claim, and (E) an overly uniform exponential lower bound. They are distinct and aligned with typical quantifier/uniformity confusions.

However, it leans toward a meta-linguistic identification task (which statement is the intended existence claim) rather than forcing substantial generative mathematical reasoning about cube-free constructions.

sketch:
Instead of proving Theorem~\ref{main} directly, the paper focuses on proving a “weaker” lemma (Lemma~\ref{weak}) “from which the full Theorem~\ref{main} easily follows [see appendix]”, by adding the assumption $\delta(G)\ge d/4$.

The stated proof approach for Lemma~\ref{weak} is: “bounding the entropy of a random ‘greedy’ embedding of $T$ into $G$ constructed in~\cite{MV}.” The introduction notes that in related entropy arguments (for $|\mathrm{Hom}(T,G)|$ and locally injective homomorphisms), “the marginal distribution at each edge of $T$ is a uniform random edge in $G$ and the conclusion is quickly established using Jensen’s Inequality.” For the injective case, it recalls that Mubayi–Verstra\"ete~\cite{MV} proved their bound “by showing the embedding is close to uniform at every edge.”

It then describes how the present paper handles the non-uniformity: “We show in subsequent section that the negative error from this is only substantial when $G$ is far from a disjoint union of cliques in which case the other naive estimates are far enough from equality to cancel it out.”

As an additional easy case (for the conjecture, not Theorem~\ref{main}), when $T$ has diameter $2$ (a star), one can apply Jensen’s inequality to
\[
|\mathrm{Inj}(T, G)| = \sum_{v \in V(G)} (d(v))(d(v)-1)\cdots(d(v)-t+1).
\]
expanded_sketch:
Instead of proving the main theorem directly, the paper focuses on proving a “weaker” lemma.

\begin{lemma}{\label{weak}}
For all integers $t > 0$, there exists a $d_0(t)$ such that if $T$ is a $t + 1$-vertex tree and $G$ is an $n$-vertex graph with average degree $d \geq d_0(t)$ and minimum degree $\delta(G) \geq d/4$, then
\begin{equation}
	|\Mon(T, G)| \geq n d(d - 1) \cdots (d - t + 1).
\end{equation}
If $T$ has diameter at least 3, then equality holds iff $G$ is the disjoint union of cliques of size $d + 1$.
\end{lemma}

In establishing the main theorem, the paper notes that it “easily follows [see appendix]” from the lemma above, by adding the assumption $\delta(G)\ge d/4$.

The stated proof approach for the lemma above is: “bounding the entropy of a random ‘greedy’ embedding of $T$ into $G$ constructed in~\cite{MV}.” The introduction notes that in related entropy arguments (for $|\mathrm{Hom}(T,G)|$ and locally injective homomorphisms), “the marginal distribution at each edge of $T$ is a uniform random edge in $G$ and the conclusion is quickly established using Jensen’s Inequality.” For the injective case, it recalls that Mubayi–Verstra\"ete~\cite{MV} proved their bound “by showing the embedding is close to uniform at every edge.”

It then describes how the present paper handles the non-uniformity: “We show in subsequent section that the negative error from this is only substantial when $G$ is far from a disjoint union of cliques in which case the other naive estimates are far enough from equality to cancel it out.”

As an additional easy case (for the conjecture, not the main theorem), when $T$ has diameter $2$ (a star), one can apply Jensen’s inequality to
\[
|\mathrm{Inj}(T, G)| = \sum_{v \in V(G)} (d(v))(d(v)-1)\cdots(d(v)-t+1).

mcq.question: Let $t$ be a positive integer. Which statement gives a conclusion of the form “there exists a threshold depending only on $t$ such that for all $(t+1)$-vertex trees $T$ and all $n$-vertex graphs $G$ with sufficiently large average degree $d$, a uniform lower bound holds for $|\mathrm{Inj}(T,G)|$ (and, when $\mathrm{diam}(T)\ge 3$, also characterizes when equality holds)?”

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
For every integer $t>0$ there exists a number $d_0(t)$ such that, if $T$ is a tree on $t+1$ vertices and $G$ is an $n$-vertex graph with average degree $d\ge d_0(t)$, then
\[
|\mathrm{Inj}(T,G)|\ge n\, d(d-1)\cdots(d-t+1).
\]
Moreover, if $T$ has diameter at least $3$, then equality holds if and only if $G$ is the disjoint union of cliques of size $d+1$.

|\mathrm{Inj}(T,G)|\ge n\,(d-t+1)^{t}.
\]
Moreover, if $T$ has diameter at least $3$, then equality holds if and only if $G$ is the disjoint union of cliques of size $d+1$.

|\mathrm{Inj}(T,G)|\ge n\, d(d-1)\cdots(d-t+1).

post_theorem_intro_text:
For weak solutions to elliptic $p$-Laplace systems, gradient higher integrability results go back to Elcrat and Meyers in \cite{Meyers}. The core principle of the proof is already the same as in our paper. First a Caccioppoli inequality and a Sobolev-Gagliardo-Nirenberg type inequality are used to obtain a reverse Hölder inequality, after which higher integrability follows from an application of Gehring's lemma. Higher integrability result similar to Theorem~\ref{HI_theorem} for elliptic $p$-Laplace systems was proven for very weak solutions by Iwaniec and Sbordone in \cite{Iwaniec_Sbordone} and independently by Lewis in \cite{Lewis_elliptic}. We mention that a conjecture in \cite{Iwaniec_Sbordone} on minimal integrability deficit for elliptic $p$-Laplace problems was  recently answered by Colombo and Tione in \cite{colombo_jems}. There is a difficulty in showing the Caccioppoli inequality for very weak solutions, as a very weak solution is not an admissible test function. This problem was overcome in \cite{Lewis_elliptic} by using a type of Lipschitz truncation based on Whitney decomposition. 

Theorem~\ref{HI_theorem} was proven for parabolic $p$-Laplace systems in \cite{KL_veryweak}. In the parabolic case, intrinsic geometry plays a role both in the Lipschitz truncation and in obtaining the reverse Hölder inequality. Based on \cite{KL_veryweak}, gradient higher integrability of very weak solutions was extended to variable exponent problem and higher order problem of $p$-Laplace type in \cite{MR4074602,verena_thesis,bogelein_li,Li}. Furthermore, corresponding arguments have been implemented in the context of Calder\'on-Zygmund type estimates in \cite{MR3928653,MR3483172} and applied to establish existence of very weak solutions for elliptic $p$-Laplace problems \cite{MR3531368,MR3500290} and linear parabolic problems \cite{MR3985550}. 
The parabolic Lipschitz truncation method has been considered also in relation to caloric approximations in \cite{MR3672391,MR4525732} and existence of solutions to fluid models in \cite{MR2668872}. 

     For parabolic double-phase problems higher integrability for weak solutions was shown in \cite{KKM,KS}. In there, phase analysis is used to distinguish whether the energy estimates of double-phase systems are perturbed into that of $p$-Laplace systems or $(p,q)$-Laplace systems depending on the pointwise value of $a$. Based on the phase division, we construct a corresponding intrinsic geometry.
 Similar phase analysis was used in \cite{KKS} to obtain standard energy estimates for weak solutions. Although a Lipschitz truncation method was applied in \cite{KKS}, the argument is different for very weak solutions.
Other recent result for parabolic double-phase problems include partial regularity in the nondegenerate case in \cite{MR4774133,kim2025boundedsolutionsinterpolativegap,MR4926910,oh2025gradient,ok2025partialregularityparabolicsystems,sen2025lipschitzregularityparabolicdouble}.

Corresponding result to Theorem~\ref{HI_theorem} for very weak solutions to the elliptic case was proved in \cite{BBK}. Obtaining the higher integrability result for very weak solutions to parabolic double-phase problems presents several new challenges. In order to show that there exists $\de_0$ satisfying Theorem~\ref{HI_theorem}, the higher integrability gained in the argument has to be quantified and independent from $\delta$. In \cite{KKM} the phase analysis in the reverse Hölder inequality argument for weak solutions is done with respect to a constant $K$ depending on the integral of the gradient. Utilizing the same argument for very weak solutions would lead to estimates depending on $\delta$. To avoid with this problem, we consider cylinders with radii bounded by a constant $R_0$ appearing in Theorem~\ref{HI_theorem} and use a new phase analysis argument.

Also in the proof of the Caccioppoli inequality there are novel challenges. In \cite{KKS} the Lipschitz truncation method is used to prove a Caccioppoli inequality for weak solutions to parabolic double-phase problems. In the argument in \cite{KKS}, the term $\Lambda|E(\Lambda)^c|$ in (\ref{def_E}) vanishes as $\Lambda \to \infty$. For very weak solutions this does not happen and finer estimates are required. In particular, we have to compare intrinsic cylinders in the Whitney decomposition with the underlying intrinsic cylinders defined in Section~\ref{sec_setup}. In our context these cylinders have different geometries and to compare them we provide a new argument in Lemma~\ref{lem_theta_2}. Our proof of the Caccioppoli inequality is self-contained. To simplify some of the arguments of previous papers, we have included the term $\tfrac{|u-u_0|}{\rho}$ in the definition of $E(\Lambda)$.              

Finally, we note that the range of $q$ in the parabolic double-phase system is not completely understood, however, the strict inequality for the upper bound of $q$ in (\ref{eq_range_q}) seems to be natural. For the elliptic case, the range of $q$ is well understood and its optimality is known. When we consider very weak solutions in the elliptic setting, the natural integrability of the gradient does not allow the borderline case, see \cite{BBK} for the details.

mcq.question:
Let $p,q$ satisfy $q<p+\frac{2\alpha}{n+2}$ and $p>2$. Consider a function $u$ that is a very weak solution in $\Omega_T$ of
\[
 u_t-\operatorname{div}\mathcal A(z,\nabla u)=-\operatorname{div}\big(|F|^{p-2}F+a(z)|F|^{q-2}F\big),
\]
with integrability deficit $\delta\in(\delta_0,1)$ and with $u\in C(0,T;L^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^N))$ (with $a\in L^\infty(\Omega_T)$ so that the quantities below make sense). Which statement gives the strongest conclusion of the form “there exists $\delta_0$ such that for all admissible $u$ (and all admissible cylinders) a uniform integral estimate holds” under these assumptions?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
There exists $\delta_0=\delta_0(\mathit{data})\in(0,1)$ such that $2-q(1-\delta_0)>0$ and such that, for every $\delta\in(\delta_0,1)$ and every very weak solution $u$ of
\[u_t-\operatorname{div}\mathcal A(z,\nabla u)=-\operatorname{div}\big(|F|^{p-2}F+a(z)|F|^{q-2}F\big)\ \text{in }\Omega_T,\]
with $u\in C(0,T;L^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^N))$, there exist constants $c\ge1$ and $R_0\in(0,1)$ with
\[c=c\big(\mathit{data},\|a\|_{L^\infty(\Omega_T)},\|H(z,|\nabla u|)+H(z,|F|)+1\|_{L^\delta(\Omega_T)}\big)
\quad\text{and}\quad
R_0=R_0\big(\mathit{data},\delta,\|H(z,|\nabla u|)\|_{L^\delta(\Omega_T)},\|H(z,|F|)\|_{L^\delta(\Omega_T)},\|u\|_{C(0,T;L^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^N))}\big),

\[

theorem.content:
\label{thm:main}
For every $v,D>0$ there exists a constant $F_{\Ein}(v,D)>0$ with the following
property.  If $(M^4,g)\in \Ee_1(4,v,D)$, then the area $A_{\min}(M,g)$ of a
smallest $2$-dimensional stationary integral varifold in $(M,g)$ satisfies
\[
 A_{\min}(M,g)\ \le\ F_{\Ein}(v,D).
\]
Moreover $F_{\Ein}(v,D)$ can be written explicitly in terms of the Sobolev
constant $C_S(v,D)$, the global $L^2$–curvature bound, and the quantitative
Einstein $\varepsilon$–regularity constants.
theorem.label: thm:main

ref_dict.thm:Ein-fill:
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:Ein-fill}
For every $v,D>0$ there exist functions $$f_1^{\Ein}(v,D),f_2^{\Ein}(v,D)>0, $$
with the following property.  If $(M^4,g)\in \Ee_1(4,v,D)$ and
$C\in\Zz_1(M;\Z)$ is a singular Lipschitz $1$-cycle, then $C$ bounds a
singular $2$-chain $E\in\Cc_2(M;\Z)$ such that
\[
 \mass_2(E)\ \le\ f_1^{\Ein}(v,D)\,\mass_1(C) + f_2^{\Ein}(v,D).
\]
Equivalently, the first homological filling function of $(M,g)$ satisfies
\[
 \HF_1(l)\ \le\ f_1^{\Ein}(v,D)\,l + f_2^{\Ein}(v,D)
 \qquad\text{for all }l\ge 0.
\]
\end{theorem}

post_theorem_intro_text:
As in \cite{LW_HF1}, the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} proceeds via a
homological filling inequality expressed in terms of the first homological
filling function $\HF_1$ of $(M,g)$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:Ein-fill}
For every $v,D>0$ there exist functions $$f_1^{\Ein}(v,D),f_2^{\Ein}(v,D)>0, $$
with the following property.  If $(M^4,g)\in \Ee_1(4,v,D)$ and
$C\in\Zz_1(M;\mathbb{Z})$ is a singular Lipschitz $1$-cycle, then $C$ bounds a
singular $2$-chain $E\in\Cc_2(M;\mathbb{Z})$ such that
\[
 \mass_2(E)\ \le\ f_1^{\Ein}(v,D)\,\mass_1(C) + f_2^{\Ein}(v,D).
\]
Equivalently, the first homological filling function of $(M,g)$ satisfies
\[
 \HF_1(l)\ \le\ f_1^{\Ein}(v,D)\,l + f_2^{\Ein}(v,D)
 \qquad\text{for all }l\ge 0.
\]
\end{theorem}

Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is then an immediate consequence of
Theorem~\ref{thm:Ein-fill} and the min–max theorem of Nabutovsky--Rotman
\cite{nabutovsky2006curvature}, which relates $A_{\min}(M,g)$ to $\HF_1$.
In the Einstein setting we can track all constants arising from the Sobolev
inequality, the $L^2$–curvature bound and the bubble–tree decomposition,
thus making $F_{\Ein}(v,D)$ completely explicit once the analytic data are fixed.

sketch:
The introduction explains that the proof of Theorem~\ref{Thm-Existence} in $\mathbb{H}^n$ cannot follow the $\mathbb{R}^n$ strategy based on scaling, since in $\mathbb{H}^n$ such transformations are lacking. The authors instead adopt a $\Phi_{\lambda}$-transformation in the upper half-space model, which allows scaling the volume of sets by adjusting $\lambda$.

Using the $\Phi_{\lambda}$-transformation, they "establish several fundamental properties of the minimizers, including their regularity, essential boundedness and indecomposability," and "further deduce the existence of minimizers for all sufficiently small volumes $m\leq m_0$" (for some $m_0$ depending on $n,\alpha,\gamma$).

For uniqueness and identification of minimizers as geodesic balls in the small-volume regime, they note a key difficulty: $\Phi_{\lambda}$ "cannot map geodesic balls to geodesic balls," so the usual fixed-volume argument from $\mathbb{R}^n$ does not apply. A "key observation" is that if a minimizer $E$ has $|E|_g=|B_r|_g=m\leq m_0$, then $E$ is contained in a slightly larger geodesic ball of radius $(1+C_3 r^{\frac{1}{2n}})r$.

Combining this containment with "a notion of quasiminimizer of the perimeter," they show $\partial E$ is "a radial graph over $\mathbb{S}^{n-1}$" with radial function close to $r$ when $m$ is small. Finally, "by means of proof by contradiction and Fuglede's type estiamtes for the perimeter and the nonlocal term," they conclude that for sufficiently small volumes $m$, geodesic balls are the unique minimizers up to hyperbolic isometries.

mcq.question: Let $\mathcal H$ be a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, and let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all probability measures supported on the closed unit ball $\{x\in\mathcal H:\|x\|\le 1\}$. For $\mu\in\mathcal P$ and an integer $n\ge 3$, let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be i.i.d. samples from $\mu$ and set the empirical measure $\mu_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$. Which statement gives the uniform (worst-case over $\mu\in\mathcal P$) two-sided bound on $\big(\mathbb E\, S_1^2(\mu,\mu_n)\big)^{1/2}$ asserted under these assumptions?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
There exist universal constants $c,C>0$ such that for every integer $n\ge 3$, with $\mu_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$ built from $n$ i.i.d. samples $X_1,\dots,X_n\sim\mu$, one has

\frac{c}{\sqrt{\log n}}\;\le\;\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal P}\Big(\mathbb E\, S_1^2(\mu,\mu_n)\Big)^{1/2}\;\le\;\frac{C\sqrt{\log\log n}}{\sqrt{\log n}}\,.

mcq.question: Assume \(p \le \frac{m-2}{2}\). For the spaces \(\mathrm{Sub}_{e_n}(P \times n, M)\), and distinguishing the cases that \(M\) is open or closed (and allowing different coefficient systems), which statement gives the existence of the relevant stabilization/transfer maps together with the exact uniform (co)homological isomorphism ranges (including the stated bounds on any auxiliary parameters)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
If \(p \le \frac{m-2}{2}\), then:

(i) If \(M\) is an open manifold, there exist stabilization maps
\[\mathrm{Sub}_{e_n}(P \times n, M) \to \mathrm{Sub}_{e_{n+1}}(P \times (n+1), M)\]
whose induced map on \(H_d\) is an isomorphism for
\[
 d \le \begin{cases}
\frac{n-1}{2}, & \text{if } p \le \frac{m-3}{2},\\[4pt]
 n-1, & \text{if } p \le \frac{m-3}{2} \text{ with } \mathbb{Z}\!\left[\tfrac12\right] \text{ coefficients},\\[6pt]
\frac{n-3}{2}, & \text{if } p = \frac{m-2}{2}.
\end{cases}
\]

(ii) If \(M\) is closed and \(\ell\) is a prime, then for each \(d\) there exist an integer \(T\) which is a power of \(\ell\) and an integer \(r\) such that for every \(n \ge r\) there are transfer maps
\[H^d(\mathrm{Sub}_{e_n}(P \times n, M), \mathbb{F}_\ell) \to H^d(\mathrm{Sub}_{e_{n+T}}(P \times (n+T), M), \mathbb{F}_\ell)\]
which are periodicity isomorphisms. Moreover one can take
\[
T \le \begin{cases}
2d+1, & \text{if } p \le \frac{m-3}{2},\\
4d+5, & \text{if } p = \frac{m-2}{2},
\end{cases}
\qquad
r \le \begin{cases}
4d+3, & \text{if } p \le \frac{m-3}{2},\\
8d+11, & \text{if } p = \frac{m-2}{2}.
\end{cases}
\]

(iii) If \(M\) is closed, the cohomology with rational coefficients stabilizes, with slope \(d \le \frac{n-2}{2}\) if \(p \le \frac{m-3}{2}\) and \(d \le \frac{n-6}{4}\) if \(p = \frac{m-2}{2}\).

\label{t:main}
  Let $q\ge4$ be a prime power and $G$ be almost simple with socle
  $S=\PSL_2(q)$, that is $S\le G\le\aut(S)$. Suppose that $G$ acts
  primitively on $\Omega$. Then for every distinct
  $\alpha, \beta\in\Omega$ there exists $s\in S$ such that
  $\alpha^s=\beta$ and $s$ fixes no point of $\Omega$.

post_theorem_intro_text:
If $G$ acts primitively on $\Omega$, then the possibilities for a point
stabilizer $S_\omega < S$ are known. While some cases are relatively
easy to handle, the more difficult ones arise when $S_\omega$ is
dihedral, or when $S_\omega$ is one of the polyhedral groups $A_4$,
$S_4$, or $A_5$. In the former case we require Hasse’s bound on the
number of points on elliptic curves over finite fields, and to rule out
the latter cases we derive trace identities for the binary polyhedral
groups $2A_4$, $2S_4$, and $2A_5$.

In some cases there are lengthy calculations which, in principle,
could be carried out by hand. Instead, we provide SageMath code at
\cite{dera_psl2_verify} that confirms the claims.

\label{t:main}
  Let $q\ge4$ be a prime power and $G$ be almost simple with socle
  $S=\PSL_2(q)$, that is $S\le G\le\aut(S)$. Suppose that $G$ acts
  primitively on $\Omega$. Then for every distinct
  $\alpha, \beta\in\Omega$ there exists $s\in S$ such that
  $\alpha^s=\beta$ and $s$ fixes no point of $\Omega$.

mcq.question: Let $q\ge 4$ be a prime power and let $G$ be an almost simple group with socle $S=\PSL_2(q)$ (so $S\le G\le \operatorname{Aut}(S)$). Suppose that $G$ acts primitively on a set $\Omega$. Under these assumptions, which of the following is the strongest conclusion that holds for arbitrary distinct points $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: For every distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega$ there exists an element $s\in S$ such that $\alpha^s=\beta$ and $s$ fixes no point of $\Omega$.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For every distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega$ there exists an element $s\in G$ such that $\alpha^s=\beta$ and $s$ fixes no point of $\Omega$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For every distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega$ there exists an element $s\in S$ such that $\alpha^s=\beta$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: For every distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega$ there exists an element $s\in S$ such that $\alpha^s=\beta$ and $s$ fixes at most one point of $\Omega$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For every distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega$ there exists an element $s\in S$ such that $\alpha^s=\beta$ and $s$ has prime order.

theorem.content:
\label{thm:main_window}
Let $u\ge 1$, $q\ge 2$ be integers, and let $\mathcal F$ be a finite family of
non-empty binary words.  Let $L=\max\{|f|:f\in\mathcal F\}$ and fix $M\ge L$.
Then the set
\[
   S_u^{(M)}=\{n\ge 0:\ uq^n\in \mathcal K_{\mathcal F}^{(M)}\}
\]
is either finite or ultimately periodic.  That is, there exist integers $n_0\ge 0$ and $p\ge 1$
such that
\[
   n\in S_u^{(M)}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ n+p\in S_u^{(M)}\qquad(n\ge n_0).
\]
Moreover, one can effectively compute such a pair $(n_0,p)$ and decide whether
$S_u^{(M)}$ is finite or infinite.  In the finite case, the same procedure
outputs all elements of $S_u^{(M)}$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main_window}
Let $u\ge 1$, $q\ge 2$ be integers, and let $\mathcal F$ be a finite family of
non-empty binary words.  Let $L=\max\{|f|:f\in\mathcal F\}$ and fix $M\ge L$.
Then the set
\[
   S_u^{(M)}=\{n\ge 0:\ uq^n\in \mathcal K_{\mathcal F}^{(M)}\}
\]
is either finite or ultimately periodic.  That is, there exist integers $n_0\ge 0$ and $p\ge 1$
such that
\[
   n\in S_u^{(M)}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ n+p\in S_u^{(M)}\qquad(n\ge n_0).
\]
Moreover, one can effectively compute such a pair $(n_0,p)$ and decide whether
$S_u^{(M)}$ is finite or infinite.  In the finite case, the same procedure
outputs all elements of $S_u^{(M)}$.
\end{theorem}

post_theorem_intro_text:
The proof is entirely finite-state.  The crucial input is the fact that
multiplication by a fixed integer $q$ in the Fibonacci numeration system is
realizable by a finite sequential transducer \cite{Frougny1992}.  Reading digits
from the least significant side, this transducer induces, for each $M$, a
deterministic update rule on the set of length-$M$ windows
$\{0,1,\#\}^M$.  After composing with the finite automaton that checks avoidance
of $\mathcal F$ inside the window, we obtain a deterministic dynamical system on
a finite state space.  The orbit associated with the progression $(uq^n)_{n\ge
0}$ is therefore eventually periodic, which yields ultimate periodicity of
$S_u^{(M)}$ as an immediate corollary.  The same finite-state construction gives
an explicit algorithm to compute the eventual period.

Theorem~\ref{thm:main_window} gives a rigorous and completely effective solution
to the window-restricted problem.  While passing from $S_u^{(M)}$ to the global
set $S_u$ entails additional difficulties (one must control where forbidden
patterns may first appear as $n$ varies), the window-restricted variant already
captures the local dynamics of Zeckendorf multiplication and provides a
practical method to detect all exponents for which the low-order Zeckendorf
digits of $uq^n$ satisfy prescribed constraints.

Under these assumptions, which of the following is the strongest conclusion about $S_u^{(M)}$ (including any algorithmic/effectivity statements)?

$S_u^{(M)}$ is either finite or ultimately periodic: there exist integers $n_0\ge 0$ and $p\ge 1$ such that for all $n\ge n_0$,

 n\in S_u^{(M)}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ n+p\in S_u^{(M)}.
\]
Moreover, one can effectively compute such a pair $(n_0,p)$ and decide whether $S_u^{(M)}$ is finite or infinite; in the finite case, the same procedure outputs all elements of $S_u^{(M)}$.

\[
 n\in S_u^{(M)}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ n+p\in S_u^{(M)}.
\]
Moreover, there is a uniform algorithm which, given only $q$, $\mathcal F$, and $M$ (but not $u$), effectively computes a pair $(n_0,p)$ that works for this $S_u^{(M)}$ for every $u\ge 1$ and decides whether $S_u^{(M)}$ is infinite.

theorem.content: For any sequence of random variables $\{d_i\}$, one can find a decoupled sequence $\{e_i\}$ (on a possibly enlarged probability space) which is tangent to the original sequence and in addition conditionally independent given a master $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{G}$. Frequently $\mathcal{G} = \sigma(\{d_i\})$.

sketch:
Specifically, with $\{d_i\}$, a tangent sequence w.r.t. $\F_i = \sigma(d_1,...,d_i)$ can be obtained via the following steps:
\begin{itemize}[noitemsep, topsep=0pt]
    \item First, we take $d_1$ and $e_1$ to be two independent copies of the same random mechanism. 
    \item With ($d_1,..,d_{i-1}$), the i-th pair of variables $d_i$ and $e_i$ comes from i.i.d. copies of the same random mechanism given $\F_{i-1}$. 
\end{itemize}
And $e_i$’s are conditionally independent w.r.t. $\mathcal{G} = \F_n$.

Specifically, with $\{d_i\}$, a tangent sequence w.r.t. $\F_i = \sigma(d_1,...,d_i)$ can be obtained via the following steps:
\begin{itemize}[noitemsep, topsep=0pt]
    \item First, we take $d_1$ and $e_1$ to be two independent copies of the same random mechanism. 
    \item With ($d_1,..,d_{i-1}$), the i-th pair of variables $d_i$ and $e_i$ comes from i.i.d. copies of the same random mechanism given $\F_{i-1}$. 
\end{itemize}
And $e_i$’s are conditionally independent w.r.t. $\mathcal{G} = \F_n$.,

mcq.question: Let $\{d_i\}$ be any sequence of random variables on some probability space. Under these assumptions, which of the following strongest conclusions holds regarding the existence of an associated sequence with decoupling and tangency properties?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: There exists a (possibly enlarged) probability space carrying a sequence of random variables $\{e_i\}$ such that $\{e_i\}$ is a decoupled sequence that is tangent to $\{d_i\}$ and, moreover, the variables $\{e_i\}$ are conditionally independent given some master $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal G$ (frequently one may take $\mathcal G=\sigma(\{d_i\})$).

choices.label: B
choices.text: There exists a (possibly enlarged) probability space carrying a sequence of random variables $\{e_i\}$ such that $\{e_i\}$ is tangent to $\{d_i\}$ and the variables $\{e_i\}$ are (unconditionally) independent; moreover one may take the master $\sigma$-algebra to be trivial, $\mathcal G=\{\emptyset,\Omega\}$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There exists a (possibly enlarged) probability space carrying a sequence of random variables $\{e_i\}$ such that $\{e_i\}$ is tangent to $\{d_i\}$.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There exists a (possibly enlarged) probability space carrying a sequence of random variables $\{e_i\}$ such that $\{e_i\}$ is a decoupled sequence tangent to $\{d_i\}$ and the variables $\{e_i\}$ are conditionally independent given $\mathcal G=\sigma(\{d_i\})$ (in particular, given $\mathcal G$ they form an i.i.d. family).

choices.label: E
choices.text: There exists a sequence $\{e_i\}$ on the original probability space (no enlargement needed) such that $\{e_i\}$ is a decoupled sequence tangent to $\{d_i\}$ and the variables $\{e_i\}$ are conditionally independent given a master $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal G$ (frequently $\mathcal G=\sigma(\{d_i\})$).

sketch_usage_meta.label: C

sketch_usage_meta.label: D
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: upgraded conditional independence to conditional i.i.d. given $\mathcal G$

sketch_usage_meta.label: E
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: removed the possibility of enlarging the probability space

ALS.justification: The stem does not state or strongly hint at the specific features in the correct option (decoupling + tangency + conditional independence given a master σ-algebra, possible enlargement). The correct answer is not telegraphed by wording or structure.

TAS.justification: The item largely functions as a theorem-recall question: for an arbitrary sequence {d_i}, it asks which existence statement holds. Although phrased as “strongest conclusion,” it is close to selecting the exact theorem statement rather than applying it in a new setting.

GPS.justification: To answer, one mainly needs to know (or reconstruct) the precise maximal form of a standard decoupling/tangency existence result and compare strength across options. This is more recognition/precision than multi-step generative reasoning.

DQS.justification: Distractors are plausible and target common over/under-strengthening errors: unconditional vs conditional independence (B), dropping decoupling/conditional independence (C), incorrectly upgrading to conditional i.i.d. (D), and removing probability-space enlargement (E). They are distinct and aligned with realistic failure modes.

theorem.label: npd

sketch:
Indeed, fix $\varepsilon>0$ and find $x\in A$ with $\widehat{x}(\varphi_{i})=a_{i}$ for all $i$ such that 
\[
\|(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})\|_{NP(A;\varphi_{1},\ldots,\varphi_{n})}>\|x\|_{A}-\varepsilon.
\]
Since the norm in the Banach algebra is larger then the spectral norm, we obtain
\[
\|x\|_{A}\geq\|\widehat{x}\|_{C(\triangle(A))}\geq\max\{|\widehat{x}(\varphi_{1})|,\ldots,|\widehat{x}(\varphi_{n})|\}=\|(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})\|_{\infty},
\]
which finishes the argument (hence $\|(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})\|_{NP(A;\varphi_{1},\ldots,\varphi_{n})}\ge \|(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})\|_\infty$).

mcq.question: Let $A$ be a commutative semisimple Banach algebra, and let $(\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_n)$ be a finite set of pairwise different linearly-multiplicative functionals. For $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n$, which of the following gives the definition of the Nevanlinna--Pick norm $\|\cdot\|_{NP(A;\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_n)}$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: $$\|(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\|_{NP(A;\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_n)}=\inf\bigl\{\|x\|_{A}:\widehat{x}(\varphi_i)=a_i\text{ for all }i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\bigr\}.$$

choices.label: B
choices.text: $$\|(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\|_{NP(A;\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_n)}=\inf\bigl\{\|\widehat{x}\|_{C(\triangle(A))}:\widehat{x}(\varphi_i)=a_i\text{ for all }i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\bigr	equiv\inf\bigl\{\|x\|_{A}:\widehat{x}(\varphi_i)=a_i\text{ for all }i\bigr\}.$$

choices.label: C
choices.text: $$\|(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\|_{NP(A;\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_n)}=\inf\bigl\{\|x\|_{A}:\widehat{x}(\varphi_i)=a_i\text{ for some }i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\bigr\}.$$

choices.label: D
choices.text: $$\|(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\|_{NP(A;\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_n)}=\sup\bigl\{\|x\|_{A}:\widehat{x}(\varphi_i)=a_i\text{ for all }i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\bigr\}.$$

choices.label: E
choices.text: $$\|(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\|_{NP(A;\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_n)}=\inf\bigl\{\|x\|_{A}:\widehat{x}(\varphi_i)=a_{\sigma(i)}\text{ for all }i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\text{ for some permutation }\sigma\in S_n\bigr\}.$$

sketch_usage_meta.label: C

theorem.content:
\label{thm:main}
Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic zero.  There do not exist Nisnevich sheaves of abelian groups $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{A}$ on \(Sm_{k}\) which are strongly (hence strictly) $\mathbb{A}^{1}-$invariant and whose evaluations on fields recover \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\), together with maps
$
\mathbb{G}_{m}\to \mathcal{P},  \mathbb{G}_{m}^{\wedge 2}\to \mathcal{A},
$
that restrict on fields to the canonical symbol maps \(z\mapsto\{z\}\) for $z\neq1$ $(1\mapsto 0)$ and \((x,y)\mapsto x\wedge y\).
theorem.label: thm:main

ref_dict.2.3:
\begin{theorem}\label{2.3}\cite{Morel12}
Let $n\geq 1$. The morphism $\sigma_{n}$ is the universal morphism from $\mathbb{G}_{m}^{\wedge n}$ to a strongly $\mathbb{A}^{1}$-invariant sheaf of abelian groups. That is, given a morphism of pointed sheaves $\phi:\mathbb{G}_{m}^{\wedge n}\rightarrow M$ where $M$ is a strongly $\mathbb{A}^{1}$-invariant sheaf of abelian groups, there exists a unique morphism of sheaves of abelian groups $\Phi$ such the following diagram commutes:

\[\begin{tikzcd}
{\mathbb{G}_{m}^{\wedge n}} \\
\\
{\textbf{K}_{n}^{MW}} &&& M
\arrow["\sigma_{n}", from=1-1, to=3-1]
\arrow["\phi", from=1-1, to=3-4]
\arrow["\Phi"', from=3-1, to=3-4]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\end{theorem}

post_theorem_intro_text:
The main ingredient of the proof is Theorem \ref{2.3} which compares objects of $SAI(Sm_{k})$ with the universal object \textbf{K}$^{MW}_{n}$ with respect to the symbol map $\sigma_{n}$. Thus, although \(K_{2}^{M}\) extends to a strongly $\mathbb{A}^{1}-$invariant sheaf, the intermediate objects \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) can not be promoted to strongly $\mathbb{A}^{1}-$invariant sheaves if one insists on extending the canonical symbol maps from \(\mathbb{G}_m\) and \(\mathbb{G}_m^{\wedge2}\).  Intuitively, the obstruction arises because \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) encode subtle five-term/dilogarithmic relations and anti-symmetric tensor structure that are incompatible with the relations in Milnor-Witt $K-$theory.

\subsection*{Acknowledgements}
This work was carried out as part of the author’s master’s thesis at the Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata, India, from January to April 2025. The author is deeply grateful to his supervisor, Dr. Utsav Choudhury, for suggesting the problem and for his constant support throughout the project.

expanded_sketch:
The post-theorem introduction says that the “main ingredient of the proof is the following theorem which compares objects of $SAI(Sm_{k})$ with the universal object \textbf{K}$^{MW}_{n}$ with respect to the symbol map $\sigma_{n}$.” We first recall this theorem.

\begin{theorem}\label{2.3}\cite{Morel12}
Let $n\geq 1$. The morphism $\sigma_{n}$ is the universal morphism from $\mathbb{G}_{m}^{\wedge n}$ to a strongly $\mathbb{A}^{1}$-invariant sheaf of abelian groups. That is, given a morphism of pointed sheaves $\phi:\mathbb{G}_{m}^{\wedge n}\rightarrow M$ where $M$ is a strongly $\mathbb{A}^{1}$-invariant sheaf of abelian groups, there exists a unique morphism of sheaves of abelian groups $\Phi$ such the following diagram commutes:

\[\begin{tikzcd}
{\mathbb{G}_{m}^{\wedge n}} \\
\\
{\textbf{K}_{n}^{MW}} &&& M
\arrow["\sigma_{n}", from=1-1, to=3-1]
\arrow["\phi", from=1-1, to=3-4]
\arrow["\Phi"', from=3-1, to=3-4]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\end{theorem}

Using this comparison/universality, the argument concludes that “although \(K_{2}^{M}\) extends to a strongly $\mathbb{A}^{1}-$invariant sheaf, the intermediate objects \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) can not be promoted to strongly $\mathbb{A}^{1}-$invariant sheaves if one insists on extending the canonical symbol maps from \(\mathbb{G}_m\) and \(\mathbb{G}_m^{\wedge2}\).” The stated intuition is that “the obstruction arises because \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) encode subtle five-term/dilogarithmic relations and anti-symmetric tensor structure that are incompatible with the relations in Milnor-Witt $K-$theory.”

\label{thm:main}
Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic zero. There do not exist Nisnevich sheaves of abelian groups $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{A}$ on \(Sm_{k}\) which are strongly (hence strictly) $\mathbb{A}^{1}-$invariant and whose evaluations on fields recover \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\), together with maps
$
\mathbb{G}_{m}\to \mathcal{P},  \mathbb{G}_{m}^{\wedge 2}\to \mathcal{A},
$
that restrict on fields to the canonical symbol maps \(z\mapsto\{z\}\) for $z\neq1$ $(1\mapsto 0)$ and \((x,y)\mapsto x\wedge y\).,

mcq.question: Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic zero. Suppose one seeks Nisnevich sheaves of abelian groups \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) on \(Sm_k\) that are strongly (hence strictly) \(\mathbb{A}^1\)-invariant, whose evaluations on fields recover \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\), and that admit maps \(\mathbb{G}_m\to \mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathbb{G}_m^{\wedge 2}\to \mathcal{A}\) restricting on fields to the canonical symbol maps \(z\mapsto\{z\}\) for \(z\neq 1\) with \((1\mapsto 0)\), and \((x,y)\mapsto x\wedge y\). Under these assumptions, which conclusion holds?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: No such Nisnevich sheaves \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) on \(Sm_k\), with the stated strong \(\mathbb{A}^1\)-invariance, field-evaluation property, and maps \(\mathbb{G}_m\to\mathcal{P}\), \(\mathbb{G}_m^{\wedge 2}\to\mathcal{A}\) restricting on fields to the indicated canonical symbol maps, exist.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Such Nisnevich sheaves \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) do exist provided one only requires them to be \emph{strictly} \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\)-invariant (not necessarily strongly \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\)-invariant), while still recovering \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) on fields and admitting maps \(\mathbb{G}_{m}\to \mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathbb{G}_{m}^{\wedge 2}\to \mathcal{A}\) restricting on fields to the canonical symbol maps \(z\mapsto\{z\}\) (with \(1\mapsto 0\)) and \((x,y)\mapsto x\wedge y\).

choices.label: C
choices.text: There do not exist Nisnevich sheaves of abelian groups \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) on \(Sm_k\) that are strongly \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\)-invariant, whose evaluations on fields recover \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\), together with maps \(\mathbb{G}_m\to\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathbb{G}_m^{\wedge2}\to\mathcal{A}\) which restrict on fields to the indicated canonical symbol maps \emph{for all fields at once}.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Such Nisnevich sheaves \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) exist, but necessarily the induced maps \(\mathbb{G}_m\to \mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathbb{G}_m^{\wedge 2}\to \mathcal{A}\) factor uniquely through the universal symbol maps \(\sigma_1:\mathbb{G}_m\to \mathbf{K}^{MW}_1\) and \(\sigma_2:\mathbb{G}_m^{\wedge 2}\to \mathbf{K}^{MW}_2\), so that on fields the canonical symbols \(z\mapsto\{z\}\) (\(1\mapsto 0\)) and \((x,y)\mapsto x\wedge y\) are recovered via the corresponding Milnor--Witt \(K\)-theory classes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No such Nisnevich sheaves \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\) exist as stated, but one can still construct a strongly \(\mathbb{A}^1\)-invariant Nisnevich sheaf \(\mathcal{A}\) extending the field-valued functor \(\mathcal{A}\) together with a map \(\mathbb{G}_m^{\wedge2}\to\mathcal{A}\) restricting on fields to \((x,y)\mapsto x\wedge y\); the obstruction concerns only the simultaneous existence of \(\mathcal{P}\) with \(\mathbb{G}_m\to\mathcal{P}\) extending \(z\mapsto\{z\}\) (\(1\mapsto 0\)).

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: For a generic Higgs bundle in $\mathcal M_{\text{Dol}}(\mathcal X/\mathcal T_g)$, its isomonodromic deformation is holomorphic along every direction in $\mathcal T_g$.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For a generic Higgs bundle in $\mathcal M_{\text{Dol}}(\mathcal X/\mathcal T_g)$, the criterion $\theta_\ast\circ\rho_{KS}(\partial/\partial t)=0$ holds for every direction $\partial/\partial t\in T\mathcal T_g$, and hence the associated isomonodromic deformation is holomorphic along any direction in $\mathcal T_g$.

\begin{conjecture}[\protect{\cite[Conjecture 5.3]{BE24}}]\label{conjec}
     For $n\geq 3$, the Gotzmann threshold $\tau_n(x_2^d)$ is a polynomial of degree $2^{n-2}$ in $d$ with the same dominant term as the $(n-2)$-iterated binomial coefficient
     \[
 \begin{pmatrix}
     \binom{\binom{d}{2}}{2}\\
     \cdots\\
     2
 \end{pmatrix},
 \]
    which is $2(d/2)^{2^{n-2}}$.
 \end{conjecture}

\label{thm:main-4-recursive}
    Given integers $n,r$ where $2\leq r<n-1$. Then the Gotzmann threshold $\tau_n(x_r^d)$ in $\Bbbk[x_1,\dots ,x_{n}]$ can be computed recursively:
    \begin{align*}
        \tau_{r+1}(x_r^d) &= \binom{d+r-1}{r}-d,\\
        \tau_{n}(x_r^d)&= \binom{d+n-1}{d} - \binom{d+n-r}{d} - \binom{d+r-1}{d} +1
            + \sum_{i=r+1}^{n-1} (-1)^{n+1-i}\binom{\tau_{i}(x_r^d)}{n+1-i}.
    \end{align*},

mcq.question: Let $n,r$ be integers with $2\le r<n-1$, and let $d$ be a positive integer. In the polynomial ring $\Bbbk[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, what is the recursive computation for the Gotzmann threshold $\tau_n(x_r^d)$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
It satisfies the base case
$$\tau_{r+1}(x_r^d)=\binom{d+r-1}{r}-d,$$
and for $n\ge r+2$ the recursion
$$\tau_{n}(x_r^d)= \binom{d+n-1}{d} - \binom{d+n-r}{d} - \binom{d+r-1}{d} +1
            + \sum_{i=r+1}^{n-1} (-1)^{n+1-i}\binom{\tau_{i}(x_r^d)}{n+1-i}.$$

            + \sum_{i=r+1}^{n-1} (-1)^{n+1-i}\binom{\tau_{i}(x_r^d)}{\,n-i\,}.$$

$$\tau_{r+1}(x_r^d)=\binom{d+r-1}{r}-d,$$
and for $n\ge r+2$ one has the lower bound
$$\tau_{n}(x_r^d)\ge \binom{d+n-1}{d} - \binom{d+n-r}{d} - \binom{d+r-1}{d} +1.$$

It satisfies the base case
$$\tau_{r+1}(x_r^d)=\binom{d+r-1}{r}-d,$$
and for $n\ge r+2$ the recursion

            + \sum_{i=r+2}^{n-1} (-1)^{n+1-i}\binom{\tau_{i}(x_r^d)}{n+1-i}.$$

choices.label: E

It satisfies the base case
$$\tau_{r+1}(x_r^d)=\binom{d+r-1}{r}-d,$$
and for $n\ge r+2$ the recursion
$$\tau_{n}(x_r^d)= \binom{d+n-1}{d} - \binom{d+n-r}{d} - \binom{d+r-1}{d} +1
            + \sum_{i=r+1}^{n-1} (-1)^{n+1-i}\binom{\tau_{n-1}(x_r^d)}{n+1-i}.$$

theorem.label: thm:charac-Markov

post_theorem_intro_text:
\begin{rmq}\label{rmq:}
  If we do not suppose that the automorphism group is non-elementary then other examples can arise. For example, if $C$
  is a curve of degree 3 in $\mathbf{P}^2$ with a nodal singularity, then $X_0 := \mathbf{P}^2 \setminus C$ is a smooth affine surface
  completable by a cycle of rational curves. Indeed, if we blow up the nodal singularity we get a completion $X$ of
  $X_0$ such that $\Delta_X = C_1 \cup C_2$ which are two smooth rational curves that meet at two points. Here
  $\Aut (X_0)$ is virtually cyclic with the generator being a loxodromic automorphism so the automorphism group is
  elementary.
\end{rmq}

\subsection{Idea of the proof}\label{subsec:}
The proof goes as follows. We use the valuative techniques from \cite{abboudDynamicsEndomorphismsAffine2023}. In the
case of an affine surface completable by a cycle of rational curves, the space of valuations centered at infinity of
$X_0$ contains an $\Aut(X_0)$-equivariant set which is homeomorphic to a circle. This circle is homeomorphic to the
completion of the inverse limits of the dual graphs of cyclic completions. If $\Aut(X_0)$ is non-elementary, then its
action on this circle has very large orbits. This imposes strong constraints on the intersection form on the space of
divisors supported at infinity. We then conclude that $X_0$ has to be the complement of a triangle of lines in a smooth
cubic surface unless $X_0 = \G_m^2$.

\subsection{Study of endomorphisms of affine surfaces of Markov type}\label{subsec:endomorphisms-intro}
We fully classify the dynamics of cubic affine surfaces of Markov type in characteristic zero by showing that they do not have
non-invertible dominant endomorphisms. 

\begin{bigthm}\label{thm:endomorphisms-affine-surface}
  Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero. If $X_0$ is a smooth cubic affine surface of Markov type over $K$ and $f$ is a
  dominant endomorphism of $X_0$, then $f$ is an automorphism.
\end{bigthm}
To show this result we can assume that $K = \mathbf{C}$, then using valuative techniques and the geometry of the space of
valuations centered at infinity we show that $f$ must be proper and unramified. Thus, it is a covering of the complex
manifold $X_0 (\mathbf{C})$ which is simply connected (see eg \cite[Lemma 3.10]{cantatHolomorphicDynamicsPainleve2007}). Hence
$f$ must be a homeomorphism and therefore an automorphism.

Notice that this is not true for singular cubic affine surfaces. Indeed, let $\sC \subset \mathbf{A}^3$ be the Cayley cubic defined by 
\begin{equation}
  x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = xyz + 4.
  \label{<+label+>}
\end{equation}
It is the quotient of $\G_m^2$ by the involution $(u,v) \mapsto (u^{-1}, v^{-1})$. The Cayley cubic has four singular
points which are orbifold singularities of order 2. It has many endomorphisms, namely every monomial endomorphism of
$\G_m^2$ descends to an endomorphism of $\sC$. The proof fails for this surface because it is not simply connected as an
orbifold. Indeed, its orbifold fundamental group is not trivial.

\subsection*{Acknowledgements} I thank Serge Cantat and Matteo Ruggiero for related discussions on this problem.

post_theorem_intro_text:
This theorem may be viewed as a cosmological singularity theorem for spacetimes compatible with a positive cosmological constant:  If the Cauchy surface has a topology other than that of a spherical space, the spacetime is past null geodesically incomplete.  De Sitter space, and certain quotients, illustrate the relevance of case~(i).  
Dust-filled FLRW models, with positive cosmological constant and with compact Cauchy surfaces of positive, negative, and zero curvature illustrate both cases. The negative and zero curvature cases do not have spherical space topology and all begin with a big bang. For a suitably chosen value of the cosmological constant, the positive curvature (i.e., spherical) case can escape a big bang singularity. See e.g.,\ 
\cite[Section~23.3]{DInverno}.

The following construction yields a class of $\Lambda$-vacuum examples of Theorem \ref{thm: main}.

\medskip

\noindent
\emph{Further examples.} Let $V$ be a compact 3-manifold. By the Yamabe problem (see \cite{Schoen1989} for a discussion), there is a Riemannian metric $h$ on $V$ with constant scalar curvature $R_h$. The $\Lambda$-vacuum Einstein constraint equations are
\[
R_h - |K|_h^2 + (\text{tr}_hK)^2 = 2\Lambda \quad \text{ and } \quad D_iK^i_{\:j} - D_jK^i_{\:i} = 0,
\]
{where $D$ is the $h$-covariant derivative. Set $K = h$. Then the second constraint is satisfied since $DK = Dh = 0$. The left-hand side of the first constraint is constant; choose $\Lambda$ so that it's satisfied. Since $K$ is positive definite, Theorem \ref{thm: main} implies that the resulting maximal globally hyperbolic development of the initial data set $(V, h, K=h)$ is past null geodesically incomplete so long as $V$ is not a spherical space.

\medskip

The proof of Theorem \ref{thm: main} in \cite{GL_topo_cosmo} made use of a deep consequence of Thurston's geometrization conjecture,  namely the positive resolution of the surface subgroup conjecture \cite{Kahn}.  In this paper, we show, alternatively, how the less-broadly-known positive resolution of the virtual positive first Betti number conjecture \cite{Agol} (another deep consequence of Thurston's geometrization conjecture), can be used to  simplify  aspects of the proof, which thereby provides a unified approach to the proof.

Our simplified proof of Theorem 1 is presented in the next section.  The proof is ultimately an application of Penrose's singularity theorem \cite{Penrose} (applied to a {\it past trapped} surface).  Recently, we studied certain {\it rigidity} aspects of Penrose's singularity theorem~\cite{GL_Penrose_rigid}.  In Section 3 we present a `rigid version' of Theorem \ref{thm: main},  whose proof makes use of a result in \cite{GL_Penrose_rigid}.

mcq.question: Let $(M,g)$ be a four-dimensional spacetime satisfying the null energy condition. Assume there exists a smooth spacelike compact Cauchy surface $V$ that is expanding in all directions (i.e., its second fundamental form $K$ is positive definite). Under these assumptions, which of the following conclusions holds?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: Either (i) $V$ is a spherical space (i.e., $V$ is topologically a quotient of $S^3$), or (ii) $M$ is past null geodesically incomplete.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Either (i) $V$ is a spherical space (i.e., $V$ is topologically a quotient of $S^3$), or (ii) $M$ is \emph{future}\u0001 null geodesically incomplete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: $M$ is either past null geodesically incomplete, or $M$ contains no past trapped surface.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either (i) $V$ is a spherical space (i.e., $V$ is topologically a quotient of $S^3$), or (ii) $M$ contains a past trapped surface.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either (i) $V$ is a spherical space (i.e., $V$ is topologically a quotient of $S^3$), or (ii) $M$ is past null geodesically incomplete, and moreover $\pi_1(V)$ has a finite-index subgroup with positive first Betti number.

sketch_usage_meta.label: B
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: time-orientation of Penrose application (past vs future trapped/incompleteness)

sketch_usage_meta.label: C
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: dropped the topological alternative by weakening to a tautological trapped-surface disjunction

sketch_usage_meta.label: D
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: replaced Penrose conclusion (incompleteness) with an intermediate hypothesis (existence of past trapped surface)

sketch_usage_meta.label: E
sketch_usage_meta.tampered_component: misstated role of virtual positive first Betti number (used in proof, not an additional conclusion forced by hypotheses)

ALS.justification: The stem does not state or strongly hint at the specific disjunction in the keyed answer; the conclusion must be selected from the options.

TAS.justification: The item is essentially a direct restatement of a known theorem in Lorentzian geometry (NEC + everywhere-expanding compact Cauchy surface implies either spherical-space topology or past null incompleteness), with minimal transformation into a choice task.

GPS.justification: Selecting among A/B/D/E requires some reasoning about the correct direction (past vs future) and what the theorem actually concludes versus what appears as an intermediate step, but for anyone who recognizes the theorem it becomes mostly recall.

DQS.justification: Distractors are plausible and target common errors: time-orientation swap (B), confusing a proof ingredient with the conclusion (D), adding an unjustified strengthening about Betti number (E), and a weaker-true but not best/strongest statement (C). They are distinct and aligned with realistic failure modes.

qa quality eval.overall_assessment: Good distractor design with little answer leakage, but the question is largely tautological (theorem-recall) rather than a genuinely generative reasoning task.

[Main theorem, informal]
    Let $X$ be a local spectral expander whose links are $\beta$-coboundary expanders. For every group $\Gamma$ and every locally minimal cochain $f : X(k) \to \Gamma$, if $\left\|f\right\| \lesssim \beta^k/(k+2)!$ then $\left\|\delta f\right\| \ge c\left\|f\right\|$, where $c = \beta^k/(k!(k+1)^4)$.

sketch:
We “found a bridge between these techniques” by arguing that a general cochain “either has a ‘global’ structure in a sense that it looks much like a cocycle or it has a ‘local’ structure in a sense that it is concentrated on links of some smaller dimension.” This case analysis is then used to “apply the local-to-global averaging operators even on general cochains and not only on cocycles.”

In the “global” case, they “deduce expansion merely by spectral arguments,” whereas in the “local” case they “deduce expansion merely by coboundary expansion of the links.” Concretely, “Propositions 3.3 and 3.4 demonstrate our case analysis of general cochains: If the cochain is ‘local’ ... we get expansion from proposition 3.3, and if the cochain is ‘global’ ... we get expansion from proposition 3.4. We prove our main theorem with these two propositions.”

In the “global” case, they “deduce expansion merely by spectral arguments,” whereas in the “local” case they “deduce expansion merely by coboundary expansion of the links.” Concretely, “Propositions 3.3 and 3.4 demonstrate our case analysis of general cochains: If the cochain is ‘local’ ... we get expansion from proposition 3.3, and if the cochain is ‘global’ ... we get expansion from proposition 3.4. We prove our main theorem with these two propositions.”
